content: Syringomas are benign tumors originating from the eccrine sweat ducts. They are most commonly found in clusters on the eyelids but can also occur in other areas such as the axilla, abdomen, chest, neck, scalp, or groin. These lesions are typically symmetrical, often multiple, and may appear in clusters. Histologically, syringomas are composed of well-differentiated ductal elements. The term syringoma is derived from the Greek word syrinx, meaning pipe or tube. Syringomas can be classified into four subtypes based on Friedman and Butler's classification: localized form, form associated with Down syndrome, generalized form (including multiple and eruptive syringomas), and familial form. The most common locations for syringomas are the upper cheeks and lower eyelids. Other frequent sites include the axilla, chest, abdomen, penis, and vulva. Rarely, syringomas may be limited to the dorsum of the hands. In the eruptive variant, multiple lesions can appear simultaneously on the chest and lower abdomen. Unilateral, linear, or nevoid lesions are rare presentations. The eruptive variant may also involve intertriginous areas and the penis. The pathophysiology of syringomas remains largely unknown. It is hypothesized that syringomas represent benign hyperplastic growths arising from the intraepidermal portion of eccrine ducts in response to an inflammatory reaction, rather than true adnexal neoplasms. Another theory suggests that a hamartoma of pluripotent stem cells may precede the pathological process of eruptive syringomas. Hormonal influences may also play a role, potentially explaining the female predominance. Additionally, a hypothesis links phosphorylase deficiency, resulting from hyperglycemia in diabetes, to glycogen accumulation in the skin and within the clear cells of syringomas. A genetic mutation in chromosome 16q22 has been associated with familial autosomal dominant syringomas. Grossly, syringomas appear as small, skin-colored or yellowish papules. Microscopically, immunohistochemical tests reveal the presence of eccrine enzymes such as leucine aminopeptidase, succinic dehydrogenase, and phosphorylase. The immunohistochemical pattern of cytokeratin expression indicates differentiation toward both the uppermost part of the dermal duct and the lower intraepidermal duct. Electron microscopy findings include ductal cells with numerous short microvilli, desmosomes, luminal tonofilaments, and lysosomes. Syringomas may be associated with other conditions, including Hailey-Hailey disease (chronic familial benign pemphigus), diabetes mellitus, Down syndrome, Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, and Nicolau-Balus syndrome. They may arise sporadically or in the context of genetic disorders. Familial syringomas are typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, often manifesting during adolescence or preadolescence and most commonly affecting the face. Syringomas associated with Down syndrome are usually located in the periorbital region, though rare cases of eruptive syringomas in Down syndrome have been reported. Clear-cell syringomas may be linked to diabetes mellitus. Syringomas must be differentiated from other conditions such as acne vulgaris, apocrine hydrocystoma, basal cell carcinoma, colloid milium, Cowden disease, Favre-Racouchot syndrome, granuloma annulare, microcystic adnexal carcinoma, milia, sebaceous hyperplasia, steatocystoma multiplex, trichoepithelioma, tuberculosis, and xanthelasma. Syringomas affect approximately 1% of the population. They are more commonly observed at puberty but can occur at any age. Females are more frequently affected than males, and there is no racial predilection. No specific risk factors for syringomas have been established. Most patients with syringomas remain asymptomatic and experience no complications. The prognosis is excellent, and with treatment, syringomas typically resolve with minimal scarring and no recurrence. A positive family history of syringomas may be present. Syringomas are usually asymptomatic, though some patients may report pruritus. On physical examination, syringomas appear as small, skin-colored or yellowish dermal papules. Eruptive syringomas may present as hyperpigmented papules on the chest, penile shaft, or vulva. Lesions may appear translucent or cystic and are generally smaller than 3 mm in diameter. There are no specific laboratory or imaging findings associated with syringomas. Diagnosis is typically made via skin biopsy. A deep biopsy is often required to rule out microcystic adnexal carcinoma. Rebiopsy may be considered for persistent or recurrent lesions. Medical therapy for syringomas includes oral isotretinoin, topical atropine, topical tretinoin, and oral tranilast. However, surgery remains the mainstay of treatment, primarily for cosmetic reasons. Patients often seek treatment for syringomas on the cheeks and eyelids. The goal of surgical therapy is to destroy the tumor with minimal scarring and no recurrence. Complete removal is often challenging, and recurrence is common due to the dermal embedding of syringomas. Surgical options include excision with primary suturing, scissor excision with secondary intention healing, electrocautery, electrodesiccation and curettage, carbon dioxide laser using the pinhole method or Er:YAG laser ablation, fractionated carbon dioxide laser ablation, cryotherapy, dermabrasion, and trichloroacetic acid application. There are no primary preventive measures for syringomas. Clinical follow-up with consideration of repeat biopsy for persistent or recurrent lesions is recommended.
